title: AI Training Foundations
positioning: Free practical foundation course with optional practice labs, readiness assessment, and Certificate of Completion.

modules.title: AI Training: Roles, Tasks & Expectations
outcomes: Explain what human AI evaluation contributes
Set realistic expectations about project availability

sections.heading: Why humans are still part of AI development
sections.body: AI systems can generate fluent text, code, summaries, images, and analyses, but fluency is not the same as quality. Human evaluators help determine whether outputs are useful, accurate, relevant, safe, and aligned with instructions.

sections.heading: Common human-feedback tasks
items: Choose the stronger of two responses
Rate an answer against a rubric
Evaluate specialist work such as coding, math, science, finance, or language

sections.heading: The task is usually narrower than the whole product
sections.body: An evaluator may be asked to judge one response using one rubric. The goal is not to redesign the AI system; it is to make a careful decision within the task instructions.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.prompt: Give me three inexpensive vegetarian dinner ideas.
sections.response: 1. Chicken tacos\n2. Vegetable pasta\n3. Lentil soup
sections.analysis: The response is well formatted, but chicken violates the vegetarian requirement. A polished response can still fail the task.

sections.heading: Acceptance is not the same as active work
sections.body: Platform eligibility, onboarding, project matching, and actual task availability are different stages. Work can vary by skills, location, demand, and customer requirements.

items: Human evaluation focuses on output quality and instruction compliance.
Strong writing does not guarantee factual or instructional correctness.
Project availability can change even after onboarding.

quickChecks.q: Which is the best example of an AI-evaluation task?
options: Comparing two model answers against a rubric
quickChecks.why: Evaluation work focuses on judging model outputs.

quickChecks.q: Does every AI-training project require programming?
quickChecks.why: Many projects focus on writing, research, languages, or general reasoning.

quickChecks.q: If a platform accepts you, is continuous work guaranteed?
quickChecks.why: Acceptance and project availability are separate.

modules.title: Reading Prompts, Rubrics & Constraints
outcomes: Break a prompt into testable requirements
Use a rubric without adding personal preferences
Distinguish hard constraints from optional preferences

sections.heading: Good evaluation begins before reading the answer
sections.body: Before judging a response, understand what the user and the rubric actually require. Many mistakes happen because evaluators remember the topic but miss a constraint.

sections.definition: A requirement that must be satisfied, such as an exact number of items, a forbidden topic, a maximum length, or a required format.
A quality that improves the answer but may not be mandatory unless the prompt or rubric makes it explicit.

sections.heading: Constraint decomposition method
items: Are there length, tone, source, date, or language requirements?

sections.heading: Example: convert the prompt into a checklist
sections.prompt: Give exactly three benefits of exercise. Each benefit must be six words or fewer. Do not mention weight loss.
sections.analysis: Checklist: exactly 3 benefits; each ≤6 words; no weight-loss reference.

sections.heading: Compare
sections.prompt: Give exactly three benefits of exercise. Each benefit must be six words or fewer. Do not mention weight loss.
sections.a: Improves cardiovascular health\nSupports better sleep quality\nCan help people lose weight
sections.b: Improves cardiovascular health\nSupports better sleep\nMay improve mood
sections.analysis: A violates the explicit prohibition on weight loss. B satisfies the main constraints.

sections.heading: When instructions conflict
sections.body: If a prompt asks for “exactly three sentences” and also “one bullet per idea” but requests five ideas, do not invent a solution silently. In real evaluation work, follow the task-specific policy for ambiguity; when allowed, flag the conflict or choose the interpretation supported by the rubric.

items: Prioritize explicit requirements over personal taste.
Treat ambiguity consistently rather than guessing differently each time.

quickChecks.q: A prompt says “exactly two examples.” The answer gives three excellent examples. Is there an instruction-following issue?
quickChecks.why: The count is an explicit constraint.

quickChecks.q: What should you do first with a complex prompt?
quickChecks.why: Understanding requirements first reduces missed constraints.

quickChecks.q: Which is usually more important?
quickChecks.why: Evaluation should follow the task criteria, not personal taste.

modules.title: Evaluating Response Quality
outcomes: Evaluate instruction following, accuracy, relevance, clarity, completeness, and support
Recognize when a response is locally correct but globally poor

sections.heading: Quality is multidimensional
sections.body: A response can be correct but irrelevant, relevant but incomplete, clear but factually wrong, or detailed but instruction-breaking. Strong evaluation considers the dimensions the task actually asks you to judge.

items.name: Instruction following
items.desc: Did it do what was requested?

items.name: Relevance
items.desc: Does it stay focused on the question?

items.name: Clarity
items.desc: Can the intended audience understand it?

items.name: Completeness
items.desc: Does it address all required parts?

items.name: Support / calibration
items.desc: Are uncertain or strong claims appropriately qualified?

sections.heading: Worked comparison
sections.prompt: Give me two advantages of remote work. Keep the entire answer under 30 words.
sections.a: Remote work can reduce commuting time and provide greater flexibility in where employees perform their work.
sections.b: Remote work has many advantages. It eliminates commuting, offers flexible schedules, lowers office expenses, helps employees relocate, and may improve productivity.
sections.analysis: A follows the requested count and stays concise. B contains useful ideas but violates the requested number.

sections.heading: Longer is not automatically better
sections.body: Extra detail can reduce relevance, violate length constraints, or introduce more opportunities for factual errors.

sections.heading: Partial completion
sections.body: If a user asks to compare two laptops on price and battery life, and the answer discusses only battery life, the answer may be accurate but incomplete.

sections.heading: Avoid “vibe scoring”
sections.body: Do not choose a response just because it sounds polished, uses sophisticated vocabulary, or agrees with your preferences. Point to observable criteria.

items: Evaluate the dimensions required by the task.
A single major instruction violation can outweigh polished writing.
More words do not automatically mean higher quality.

quickChecks.q: Which dimension asks whether the response stays focused on the user’s actual request?
quickChecks.why: Relevance is about focus and usefulness to the requested task.

quickChecks.q: A response is factually accurate but fails half the requested comparison. What is the clearest issue?
quickChecks.why: It does not cover all requested parts.

quickChecks.q: Should a longer response automatically score higher?
quickChecks.why: Length can add irrelevant or risky content.

modules.title: Comparing and Ranking AI Responses
outcomes: Separate severity from number of issues

sections.heading: Pairwise evaluation is not a popularity contest
sections.body: When comparing two answers, judge both against the same requirements. Avoid deciding that one is “better” before checking each response independently.

sections.heading: A reliable comparison workflow
items: Compare issue severity, not just issue count
Choose A, B, or tie if the rubric allows

sections.heading: One major error can matter more than several minor ones
sections.body: A response with perfect formatting but a critical factual error may be worse than a response with a small style issue.

sections.heading: Example
sections.prompt: Explain photosynthesis in one sentence for a 10-year-old.
sections.a: Photosynthesis is the biochemical process through which photoautotrophic organisms synthesize glucose using electromagnetic radiation.
sections.b: Photosynthesis is how plants use sunlight to make the food they need to grow.
sections.analysis: B better matches the requested audience while remaining broadly accurate and concise.

sections.heading: Justification template
items: Evidence: It uses age-appropriate language while A relies on technical jargon.
Impact: It better satisfies the user's audience requirement.

sections.heading: Tie discipline
sections.body: If both responses satisfy the rubric similarly, do not invent a difference just to avoid a tie. Use the task's tie policy.

items: Evaluate A and B independently first.
Use ties only when the rubric permits and the quality is genuinely similar.

quickChecks.q: Which is the best first step in pairwise evaluation?
quickChecks.why: The constraints define what success means.

quickChecks.q: A has one major factual error. B has two minor style issues. Which can reasonably be better?
options: A because it has fewer issues
quickChecks.why: Issue severity matters more than raw issue count.

modules.title: Factuality, Research & Hallucinations
outcomes: Use source quality appropriately when research is permitted

sections.heading: Fluent language can hide weak factual grounding
sections.body: AI can generate plausible names, dates, quotations, statistics, citations, or explanations that are wrong. Evaluators must learn which claims deserve verification.

sections.heading: High-verification claims
items: Claims about what a company currently offers

left.title: Verifiable factual claim
items: The policy took effect on January 1.

right.title: Subjective / predictive
items: This company will definitely dominate next year.

sections.heading: Mixed-quality claim
sections.response: Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone in 1876 and was the only person developing telephone technology at the time.
sections.analysis: The second clause is an overbroad historical claim. A response can contain both reasonable and misleading components.

sections.heading: When research is allowed
items: Identify the exact claim to verify
Check publication/update date for current claims
Distinguish source evidence from your interpretation
Do not use one weak source to support an extraordinary claim
If reliable verification is unavailable, reflect uncertainty rather than inventing certainty

sections.heading: High-stakes domains need extra care
sections.body: Medical, legal, financial, and safety claims often require careful sourcing and appropriate uncertainty. The evaluator should follow the task's domain-specific rubric.

items: Check current claims against current sources when research is allowed.
Qualify uncertainty instead of inventing certainty.

quickChecks.q: Which statement most clearly needs verification?
options: U.S. unemployment was exactly 4.1% in June.
quickChecks.why: It is a precise externally verifiable statistic.

quickChecks.q: If a quote cannot be found in reliable sources, what is a reasonable concern?
options: It may be fabricated or misattributed
quickChecks.why: AI systems can invent or misattribute quotes.

quickChecks.q: What is generally preferable for verifying a current government rule?
quickChecks.why: Primary authoritative sources are stronger for current rules.

modules.title: Writing, Style & Evaluation Justifications
outcomes: Separate style preferences from rubric violations
Use evidence instead of vague criticism

sections.heading: A good decision is easier to trust when the reasoning is clear
sections.body: Many evaluation tasks ask for a short explanation. The goal is not to write an essay; it is to identify the most important evidence supporting your judgment.

sections.heading: Decision → Evidence → Impact
items: Decision: state which response is stronger or what issue exists
Impact: explain why that detail matters under the rubric

right.title: Strong
items: Response A is stronger because it answers both requested parts, while Response B addresses only the first.
The response uses technical jargon even though the user requested a beginner explanation.

sections.heading: Tone and audience
sections.body: If the user asks for a professional email, slang may be inappropriate even if the message is understandable. If the user asks for a friendly text to a close friend, a highly formal tone may be less suitable.

sections.heading: Do not over-penalize harmless style differences
sections.body: If the rubric does not care whether a response uses bullets or short paragraphs, your personal preference should not become a quality defect.

items: Explain the most important reason, not every possible nitpick.
Differentiate rubric violations from personal style preferences.

quickChecks.q: Which feedback is stronger?
options: The response does not answer the second part of the user's question.
quickChecks.why: It identifies a specific observable issue.

quickChecks.q: Should personal preference override the rubric?
quickChecks.why: Evaluation should follow the rubric.

quickChecks.q: What comes after evidence in the suggested framework?
quickChecks.why: Decision → Evidence → Impact.

modules.title: Safety, Uncertainty & Responsible Judgment
outcomes: Recognize when a response needs cautious handling
Know when a task-specific safety rubric should control the decision

sections.heading: Some answers carry more risk than others
sections.body: A minor wording issue in a recipe is different from an unsupported claim about medication, legal obligations, finances, or physical safety. Evaluation should account for the task's safety requirements and potential impact.

sections.definition: Matching the confidence of a statement to the strength of the available evidence.

left.title: Overconfident
items: This definitely means you have condition X.

right.title: Calibrated
items: That symptom can have multiple causes; a qualified clinician can assess it.
Investments involve risk, and returns are not guaranteed.

sections.heading: Responsible evaluation questions
items: Does the response claim certainty without evidence?
Does it encourage unsafe or deceptive behavior?
Does the task include a specific safety policy?

sections.heading: Follow the task-specific policy
sections.body: General intuition is not a substitute for the explicit safety or domain rubric supplied by a project.

sections.heading: Uncertainty
sections.body: If reliable sources disagree or information is incomplete, a response that clearly communicates uncertainty can be better than one that invents a definitive answer.

items: Use the project's safety/domain policy as the source of truth.

quickChecks.q: Which statement is better calibrated?
options: This investment carries risk and returns are not guaranteed.
quickChecks.why: It acknowledges uncertainty and risk.

quickChecks.q: In a high-stakes task, what should control the evaluation?
quickChecks.why: The explicit rubric is the source of truth.

modules.title: Task Workflow, Quality & Getting Started
outcomes: Recognize common opportunity and account red flags

sections.heading: Consistency is a skill
sections.body: Strong evaluators do not rely only on intuition. They use repeatable steps so that similar cases receive similar treatment.

sections.heading: A simple evaluation workflow
items: Review the full response before scoring
Verify claims when the task permits and requires it
Write a concise justification if required
Review the submission for missed constraints

right.title: Better
items: I have two years of experience using Python for backend APIs, automation scripts, and data-processing tasks.

sections.heading: Red flags
sections.body: Be cautious with guaranteed acceptance, guaranteed income, account selling, identity misrepresentation, someone offering to complete assessments for you, password requests, or promises of continuous tasks.

sections.heading: Keep expectations realistic
sections.body: Completing this course or a third-party onboarding process does not guarantee work. Use the course to improve your judgment and decision-making, not as a promise of income.

items: Accuracy and consistency matter more than speed alone.
Avoid shortcuts that violate platform or identity rules.

quickChecks.q: What should happen before scoring a response?
options: Read the task instructions and extract criteria
quickChecks.why: The task criteria define the evaluation.

quickChecks.q: Which profile statement is more useful?
options: I have two years using Python for backend APIs and automation.
quickChecks.why: Specific, accurate experience communicates fit better.

quickChecks.q: Which is a red flag?
options: A platform asks you to read task instructions
Someone guarantees account acceptance for payment
quickChecks.why: Guaranteed acceptance for payment is a serious warning sign.

landingOutcomes: Break complex prompts into clear requirements
Evaluate instruction following, accuracy, relevance, clarity, and completeness
Identify factual claims that require verification
Apply responsible judgment to higher-risk content
Use a repeatable workflow for assessments and project tasks
